blocks.heading: Specialisation and trade
blocks.text: Trade is the buying and selling or exchange of goods and services. Specialisation and trade support each other: concentrating on some activities leaves other needs to be met through exchange, while access to a wider market can make specialisation worthwhile. Selling output can provide the income needed to buy inputs or other products. Trade still depends on reliable supply, demand and acceptable terms.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Omuti Foods specialises in bread and purchases flour and repair services from other invented local suppliers. The bakery does not need to grow grain and repair every machine itself. It can sell bread and use revenue to buy those inputs and services. This allows attention to be focused on baking, but creates dependence on suppliers. If flour deliveries become unreliable, the benefits of concentration may be reduced. Trade is the exchange linking specialised activities; it is not another name for the specialisation itself.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Specialisation, trade and stakeholder effects
blocks.text:
Etango Bakes is an invented small bakery serving cafés. Most orders are standard rolls. It buys flour and packaging from other businesses and is considering dividing its work into narrower tasks.

Evaluate whether Etango Bakes should introduce narrower specialised tasks. Present a decision plan using specialisation, trade and the dependence between production stages. [12]

Knowledge: specialisation concentrates activity; division of labour divides production tasks; trade exchanges output and inputs. Application: standard café orders give repeated tasks, while flour and packaging come from other firms. Analysis: repetition may improve speed and skill, but late inputs or a stalled stage can interrupt output. Alternative: broader worker roles offer flexibility but involve more switching and a wider range of skills. Judgement: introduce a limited division of labour where the repeated work is sufficient, with planned cover and reliable suppliers. A narrow task should not be adopted merely because it looks efficient if it creates an uncovered bottleneck.
